frase_gancho.texto: A pine house that fits together like a puzzle, without a single nail.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the house we move on to the festival. Look for a wooden mask painted pink, with an almost toothless smile, deep wrinkles and a head of white hair.

guion_corto.texto: This wooden house is a troje, the traditional dwelling of the Purépecha highlands, in Michoacán. It is made of thick pine planks, joined with wooden joints, without a single nail. It has a high, four-sided roof made of thin wooden shingles called tejamanil. Notice that it has two levels. Below is the main room, where the family lives, sleeps and keeps its altar. Above, in the loft, the ears of corn from the harvest are stored, dry and protected from moisture. The troje is both house and granary, and it shows how the pine forest becomes the home of an entire family.

guion_largo.texto:
If in the first hall upstairs you saw a house of rods and mud, here you have the other great solution: the wooden house. Each region uses what its landscape provides. In the highlands of Michoacán, what abounds is pine trees, and the Purépecha learned to work them with remarkable skill. The troje is the result.

It deserves a slow look. The planks are cut by hand and joined with notches and tenons: each piece fits into another, as in a wooden puzzle, and the weight of the structure holds everything in place. Not a single nail is needed. This technique makes it possible to take a troje apart and put it back together somewhere else, and it is the reason this one could be installed inside the museum. Many trojes are still standing after decades, because pine wood, well cut and well cared for, endures.

It is said that the troje in this hall was assembled here with carpenters from the region itself, like other houses on the Upper Floor. That was the museum’s idea in the 1960s: that they would not be copies made by others, but houses raised by those who know how they are made. In this way, the wood you see holds the hand of its builders.

The word “troje” means, in Spanish, granary, and it already tells you what the upper part was for. Many trojes also have a corridor at the front, with beams and columns of carved wood, where people work, chat and dry seeds.

Notice that it has two levels. Below, people live, and above, in the loft, the corn is stored. In some regions of central Mexico, corn is kept in clay cuescomates; here it is kept in wood, and up high, where the air circulates and the moisture does not reach. Each region has its own way of protecting the same treasure.

If you could go inside, you would also see the family altar: images of saints, flowers, candles. For many Purépecha families, the house is also a small temple. Children are born there and the dead are waked there, and the space holds that continuity of lives, just as the hearth held that of the wattle-and-daub house.

The region where this troje comes from is a land of volcanoes. In nineteen forty-three, in a cornfield in the highlands, near the town of Angahuan, a volcano suddenly was born, the Paricutín. It grew for nine years and buried entire towns under lava and ash. Its ash fell as far as Mexico City. Of the town of San Juan Parangaricutiro, only the tower of its church remained. The people of the area saw it being born and still tell the story.

And here wood remains a specialty. In Paracho, a town on the plateau, guitars have been made for centuries, and its workshops are famous around the world. It is as if the pine of the highlands had found many ways to become art: a house, an instrument, a mask. In the next piece you will see another one.

texto.Region: Purépecha Plateau and highlands of Michoacán
texto.Technique/Material: Pine wood joined with mortise and tenon, wooden shingles and stone base
texto.Function: Traditional dwelling, sacred granary, family altar and ritual space

texto.pregunta: Myth: Traditional Indigenous houses were all made of mud and straw.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Each region uses what it has. In the Purépecha highlands, houses are built with pine planks, joined without nails, and with two levels: house below, granary above.
